entry.title: How Does Your Clock Set Itself?
entry.summary: Somewhere in your home, there might be a clock that nobody has ever set. It survives power cuts. It changes for daylight saving time on its own, in the middle of the night. It has no internet connection. No Wi-Fi, no GPS, no app on your phone. All it has is a tiny radio receiver, and once every second, it hears a single pulse. So how does a clock turn one pulse per second into the exact time, the date, and even the day of the week? This video goes through DCF77 near Frankfurt and WWVB in Colorado, how a radio wave carries zeros and ones, why a whole minute carries only fifty-nine bits, the parity bits that catch interference, the strange problem of when the time actually changes, daylight saving time and leap seconds, the weather forecasts hidden in the same signal, why many clocks only listen at night, which way the antenna should point, the atomic clocks behind the transmitter, and why a clock built for Germany can't make sense of Colorado.

entry.title: Why Is Flying So Safe Now?
entry.summary: In the early 1970s, every time you boarded a passenger plane, your chance of dying on that flight was about one in three hundred and fifty thousand. Today, it's about one in fourteen million. In a single lifetime, flying has become roughly forty times safer, and not because planes stopped breaking. Engines still fail. Sensors still freeze. Pilots still make mistakes. Almost every rule on a modern flight exists because somebody, somewhere, died. But people die on roads too, and roads haven't become anything like forty times safer. So how does aviation manage to learn so well? This video goes through the Boeing bomber that crashed because of a forgotten lock, the de Havilland Comets that broke apart in mid-air and a fuselage tested in a tank of water, the young Australian scientist behind the black box, the radio call that was lost at Tenerife and the single word that changed after it, the DC-10 that lost all three hydraulic systems over Iowa, Air France 447 and what happens when the autopilot switches off, a warning that never reached TWA, Swiss cheese, and the Boeing 737 MAX.

entry.title: Why Do Humans Keep Inventing Drugs?
entry.summary: More than twelve thousand years ago, in what is now Utah, someone sat by a fire and left behind a few tobacco seeds. About eight thousand years ago, people in the Andes were chewing coca leaves. And about nine thousand years ago, in a village in China, people were brewing a drink from rice, honey and fruit. These people never met, and yet each of them found a plant that changes how a human brain works. Why does every human society find a way to change its own mind? And why does a plant contain a molecule that fits a human brain at all? This video goes through caffeine-fed caterpillars and bees, how drugs led scientists to the brain's own opioids and cannabinoids, what dopamine really does, the mutation that let our ape ancestors break down alcohol, why most people who try a drug don't get hooked, coffee bans in Mecca and England, the pharmacist who isolated morphine, the Bayer chemist who made aspirin and heroin eleven days apart, the legal loophole of new psychoactive substances, and psilocybin on prescription in Australia.

entry.title: How Precise Can Time Actually Be?
entry.summary: In a laboratory in Boulder, Colorado, there is a clock so precise that over the entire age of the universe, its uncertainty would add up to less than a second. And every generation of clocks has been better than the last. So how far can this go? Is there a point where the problem isn't the clock any more, but time itself? In 2025, physicists in Rome and Budapest published a calculation that puts a crack in the idea of perfectly sharp time. This video goes through how a clock actually works, how gravity changes the rate of time (measured over thirty-three centimetres, and then across a single millimetre), the measurement problem at the heart of quantum mechanics, collapse models, the idea of Roger Penrose and Lajos Diósi that gravity forces nature to choose, and what all of that would mean for every clock in the universe, including a twist nobody would have guessed.

entry.title: Why Can't Governments Quit Microsoft?
entry.summary: By May 2025, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court had lost access to his email. Not because of a hack. The United States had put him under sanctions, and his email ran on Microsoft, an American company. Now scale that up to a whole country: tax offices, hospitals and police all depend on software from a handful of companies abroad. Governments know this, and they keep signing the contracts anyway. So why can't governments quit Microsoft? This video goes through the Czech government's framework agreement for Microsoft products, why picking the software everyone already knows was the sensible decision, what vendor lock-in looks like inside a ministry, the British government's surprising advice on lock-in in the cloud, what the CLOUD Act means for data stored in Europe, what Microsoft France told the French Senate under oath, Munich's LiMux, Schleswig-Holstein's move to open source, and a simple test any government can run on itself.

entry.title: Why Does Windows Only Have One Desktop?
entry.summary: Picture switching on a Windows PC and finding no taskbar, no Start button and not a single icon on the desktop. Your programs, drivers and files are exactly where you left them. Only the desktop has changed, and the switch that changes it is a single setting. So why does Windows only have one desktop? This video goes through the setting that decides what your desktop is, the two jobs Explorer does, the replacement desktops people bought in the early nineties, LiteStep and the community that grew up around it, Blackbox, bbLean and Emerge Desktop, Cairo Desktop and Seelen UI on Windows 11 today, and an official Microsoft feature you may have used on a ticket machine without knowing. This isn't a how-to: changing the Shell value without a working replacement can leave you with no desktop at all.

entry.title: What Happens to Open Source When AI Can Find Every Bug?
entry.summary: 948. That's how many separate ways an AI found to take over a Linux computer from the inside, each one starting as an ordinary user with no special rights. Linux code is public, and for decades that was the argument for why it's safe. So if a machine can read public code and turn it into working exploits at this scale, should software keep its code secret after all? This video goes through OpenAI's test run on the Linux kernel, Microsoft's record month of security fixes, the Heartbleed bug that sat in public code for two years, what an AI can do with a Windows patch and no source code, why the Linux kernel now treats bugs found with AI as public, and the two months between a Windows fix and WannaCry.

entry.title: Why Can't You Stop Scrolling?
entry.summary: Ten yellow pens on a table. Some of them will give you an electric shock. Nobody will tell you which. Students waiting for an experiment clicked them anyway, just to find out. So why can't you stop scrolling? Doomscrolling means carrying on through bad news, even though you know it's making you feel worse. This video goes through more than twenty thousand headline tests, a game with two rocks and a hidden snake, the designer who came up with infinite scroll, 806 Twitter users and two versions of their feed, and the Boston Marathon bombing. And it ends with what you can actually do about it.

entry.title: What Can a Hypnotist Actually Make You Do?
entry.summary: A researcher tells you that the number six no longer exists. Asked to count to ten, some people simply skipped it. That was real research. So what can a hypnotist actually make you do? Films say a hypnotist can send you out to kill, wipe a memory or plant a command for later. All of that has been tested in a lab, and the best experiments added people who were told to fake hypnosis. This video goes through a rattlesnake behind glass, a beaker of real nitric acid, a secretary in a waiting room, a test where reading stops, a bus driver in Chowchilla and a night that never happened. And it ends where hypnosis clearly does help.

entry.title: Where Did the Idea of Hell Come From?
entry.summary: Hell has an address. It's a valley just below the walls of old Jerusalem. You can walk through it today, and in 1987 Bob Dylan played a concert there. So how did that valley become a place of fire for the wicked? The older books of the Bible don't have a hell at all. This video follows how the idea came together over thousands of years: a court in Egypt, a sentence in Plato, a motive in Judea, a valley outside Jerusalem, and pictures from a book that came very close to being in the Bible. It doesn't tell you whether hell is real. No historian can.

entry.title: Why Can't You Read Your Own Body's Logs?
entry.summary: When your computer crashes, you open the logs. When your body goes wrong, you get a headache, a vague feeling and no explanation. It's your own body, and you can't ask it what happened last night. Why not? This video follows the evidence: a builder in agony with a completely unharmed foot, a construction worker with a nail in his brain and a toothache, the rule Google's engineers use to decide what may wake them up, the alarm that can watch the wrong number, the alert that carries the wrong address, and the organ that can't feel pain in its own tissue.

entry.title: Why Hasn't Big Tech Replaced Linus Torvalds?
entry.summary: Google, Microsoft, Intel, Amazon and Meta all depend on Linux. When their engineers want to change it, they send their work to one man who doesn't work for any of them, and wait for his answer. They can't fire him. They can't overrule him. So why haven't they replaced him? This video follows the code: how many of the latest nineteen thousand changes Linus wrote himself, what happened when Google kept its own branch of the kernel for Android, how a change travels through thousands of maintainers before it reaches him, who actually pays his salary, what happened when he took a whole file system back out of Linux, and what the project did the one time he stepped away.

entry.title: We Built Flying Cars. So Why Don't We Use Them?
entry.summary: This car has a certificate that says it's allowed to fly. In 1956, the American government certified another one, and only six were ever built. We were promised flying cars, and we built them, again and again. So why doesn't anyone use them? This video starts with just one flying car: why a car and a plane want almost opposite things, the 1947 flying car whose wing you were meant to rent at the airport, how much more power it takes to hover than to drive, why a helicopter gets away with it, what batteries can and can't do, and who would actually fly the thing. Then it puts a few thousand of them over one city, and keeps going.

entry.title: Why Is the B-52 Still Flying, 70 Years Later?
entry.summary: The last B-52 left the factory in 1962. In some American families, three generations have flown in it, and the US Air Force plans to keep it flying into the 2050s. It has already outlived the bomber that was meant to replace it. So why does the most powerful air force in the world keep flying its oldest bomber? This video follows the B-52 from a weekend in a Dayton hotel in 1948, where Boeing engineers redesigned it and carved a balsa model, through three completely different jobs: flying high into the Soviet Union, flying low under the radar, and carrying cruise missiles. Along the way: the XB-70 Valkyrie, a test flight that lost most of its tail fin, why a wing wears out by flying rather than by age, a bomber brought back from the Arizona desert, and why the new B-52J keeps eight engines instead of four.

entry.title: How Did 8-Bit Computers Load Games Faster?
entry.summary: Same computer. Same kind of cassette. Same program. One version loads in half the time. Nothing in the hardware changed, so what did? This video looks at turbo loaders on 8-bit home computers: how a ZX Spectrum game could load at twice the normal speed, why the Spectrum didn't do that by itself, and how a computer that only understands the slow format loads the program that teaches it the fast one. Along the way: Speedlock and why speed wasn't its only job, a Commodore 64 cassette beating a floppy disk, Atari owners in Czechoslovakia opening up their tape recorders, and a Sharp MZ-800 program that could load games the computer itself refused. The loading sounds in this video were generated from the real loading routines, a copy of the Spectrum's ROM loader with the constants Skool Daze used, and checked in an emulator. The whole turbo tape plays at the end.

entry.title: Why Are iPhone Texts to Android Still Green?
entry.summary: Send a message from one iPhone to another and it shows up blue. Send the same message to an Android phone and it turns green. In 2024 the iPhone finally got support for the same modern messaging standard Android phones use, so why are the bubbles still green? This video follows the two roads a message can take: why green was there first and blue came later, what falling back to the old road did to group chats, videos and reactions, and why the colour became a social thing in America while most of the world barely noticed. Along the way: emails from a court case showing Apple executives discussing iMessage on Android back in 2013, "Buy your mom an iPhone", Google's long line of messaging apps, RCS, Beeper Mini, and what changed in 2023 and 2024.

entry.title: How Did a 160-Character Message Become a Gold Mine?
entry.summary: In the early 2000s, mobile operators were selling data at a price that sounds absurd today: more than seven hundred dollars a megabyte. Not mobile internet. Text messages. So how did a tiny side feature of the mobile network become a gold mine? And why was every message limited to exactly 160 characters? This video follows the text message from a typewriter in 1985 to the phone in your pocket: where the number 160 really came from, why a single accented letter could cut your message by more than half, what the very first text said, and how a message could wait for a phone that was switched off. Along the way: free texting from operators' own websites, why MMS was the awkward teenager of messaging, how internet messaging apps bypassed the gold mine, and why SMS still carries your login codes when nothing else works.

entry.title: What Would a Spoonful of a Neutron Star Do?
entry.summary: On Earth, a single teaspoon of neutron-star matter would weigh billions of tonnes, several times the mass of every person alive. How can that much mass fit into a teaspoon? And if you could somehow bring a spoonful here, what would it actually do? This video works through it layer by layer: why ordinary matter is mostly empty space, what keeps an atomic nucleus from flying apart, how a dying star crushes a core the size of the Earth down to the size of a city in less than a second, and what the thing left behind is really made of. Along the way: nuclear pasta, the collision of two neutron stars that telescopes all over the world turned to watch in 2017, where some of the gold on Earth may have come from, why the three quarks inside a proton add up to only about one percent of its mass, and a number with no units that nobody can explain.

entry.title: Why Is Getting to Orbit So Hard?
entry.summary: In July 1969, the rocket that carried the crew of the first Moon landing weighed about 2,900 tonnes on the launch pad. Eight days later, what came back to Earth weighed just under five. About one part in six hundred of that rocket came home. So where did the rest go, and why does reaching space take so much? This video works through it step by step: why adding fuel to a rocket stops helping at some point, the equation every rocket still has to obey, how fast you actually need to go to stay in orbit, why rockets throw parts of themselves away on the way up, and why we can't simply build a better engine. Along the way: a schoolteacher from Kaluga, a British mathematician working on military rockets in 1813, a Falcon 9 that delivers about four percent of its launch mass, an ion engine whose push is about the weight of a sheet of paper resting on your hand, and what the same calculation says about a planet ten times heavier than Earth, and about Mars.

entry.title: Why Do We Still Write Code?
entry.summary: Here is a complete requirement for a piece of business software: "A user can cancel an order." Six words. Any developer would nod. And yet it leaves almost every real question open. After the invoice has gone out? After the order has shipped? What about the supplier? What if two people act in the same second? Today there is a tempting idea: write only the specifications, keep them in documents, review them, and let an AI write the code. It's a good idea. It's also not a new one. This video follows nearly seventy years of attempts to raise the level at which we tell computers what to do, and asks what is really different this time. Along the way: the 1957 paper that called FORTRAN an "automatic coding system", CASE tools and fourth-generation languages, Model Driven Architecture, low-code, a survey of 450 people who actually used model-driven development, Edsger Dijkstra's short note on "the foolishness of natural language programming", and a bug in Amazon's DynamoDB that took thirty-five steps to trigger.

entry.title: Why Does a New Disk Need Formatting?
entry.summary: You buy a brand-new one terabyte drive and format it with ext4, the standard filesystem on many Linux computers. Before you've saved a single file, about seventeen gigabytes are gone. Nothing has been stored yet. So what's taking up all that space? And why does a drive need formatting in the first place? This video builds the answer from the bottom up: what a drive actually offers a computer, what formatting adds on top of it, and what happens on the disk when you save one tiny file called hello.txt, when you delete it, and when the power cuts out halfway through saving. Along the way: a notebook with a thousand pages, why a five-byte file takes up 4,096 bytes, why moving a huge file can be instant, why a deleted file can sometimes be recovered (and why that's less likely on an SSD), what a journal is for, and how ext4, NTFS and Btrfs make different choices about the same job.

entry.title: Why Does Almost Every Culture Have Gods?
entry.summary: A child is left alone in a room with a game that is almost impossible to win honestly. Before the game, the researcher points to an empty chair and says an invisible princess is sitting in it. Then he leaves, and reminds the child that she is watching. Almost every culture we know of has spirits, ancestors or gods. But for most of human history, the greatest gods people believed in probably weren't moral judges. So this video asks two questions: why do humans imagine invisible minds so easily, and when did those minds start watching us? Along the way: a puppet show with a baby mouse and an alligator, hunter-gatherer societies whose high gods mostly stayed out of human affairs, the psychologist Ara Norenzayan's idea of "big gods", a coin game played with 591 people in eight communities from Fiji to Tanzania, and a huge study that tried to settle which came first: big gods or big societies.

entry.title: Why Do Banks Still Run on 60-Year-Old Code?
entry.summary: Add one penny to £999.99 in the wrong COBOL field and the answer is zero. No error message, no crash. That isn't a bug. It's a rule, and many of the world's banks still run on rules like these. COBOL is a programming language from 1959. So why haven't banks replaced it, when they have the money and the engineers? This video looks at why a rewrite is not a translation, how a meeting at the Pentagon gave business its common language, and three real cases: a British bank that tried to leave its old system, an Australian bank that managed it, and a pandemic crisis in New Jersey where everyone blamed COBOL.

entry.title: When Does Society Become the Problem?
entry.summary: Imagine waking up tomorrow and discovering that the way the world sees you has become a problem. Not because you have hurt anyone, but because you don't fit the expectations of the people around you. This video looks at what research says about suicide among transgender people, and what it can and cannot tell us. A Danish study that followed an entire national population over four decades. The difference between gender dysphoria and transgender identity, and how ICD-11 and the American psychiatric manual treat each. Minority stress, and how hundreds of small experiences can add up. A large survey of LGBTQ+ young people in the United States, and what it found among those who felt accepted. And the question of what society is responsible for, when we cannot remove every source of someone's pain, but can choose not to add to it. This is the fifth and final video in a series about transgender people. The earlier ones asked why there suddenly seem to be so many trans people, how you know you're trans, why trans people change their bodies, and why it is so hard to be trans.

entry.title: How Did a Music Cassette Store a Computer Game?
entry.summary: In the 1980s, millions of kids pressed play on an ordinary cassette recorder and listened to a screech. It wasn't music, and it wasn't a sound effect. It was the game itself, travelling as sound. This video follows one program from the tape into a ZX Spectrum: how a zero and a one became two notes an octave apart, what the steady hum before every game was for, why loading screens appeared in such a strange order, and how a single byte at the end could throw away five minutes of waiting. Along the way: why American kids mostly never heard the noise, how the Commodore 64 and Atari did it differently, the tiny screwdriver everyone used on their tape head, and the radio and TV stations that broadcast software over the air. The loading signal in this video was generated from the Spectrum's own ROM timing, and a real Spectrum program is inside. It plays in full under the closing credits. Record it, and a Spectrum (or an emulator) will load it.

entry.title: Why Is It So Hard to Be Trans?
entry.summary: Before you say a word, people have already decided whether you are a man or a woman. Most of the time, nobody notices this happening. But what happens when the way people see you doesn't match who you are? This video looks at what it is like to be transgender in a world that judges from the outside. What passing means, and why it is not proof of anyone's identity. Who decides what a man or a woman should look like. How harassment, and the possibility of it, shapes ordinary decisions, and what the largest survey of trans people in the United States found. How rejection by family, at work or in healthcare can make everyday life harder. Why so many questions asked publicly about trans people are about their bodies. And why being transgender is not information that automatically belongs to everyone who meets you. This is the fourth video in a series about transgender people. The earlier ones asked why there suddenly seem to be so many trans people, how you know you're trans, and why trans people change their bodies. The final one asks: when does society become the problem?

entry.title: Why Do Trans People Change Their Bodies?
entry.summary: Imagine choosing surgery not because of an injury, and not because of an illness that shows up on a scan, but because something about your own body feels profoundly wrong. Imagine taking medication for years, knowing it will change you in ways you cannot fully predict. Why would anyone choose that? This video looks at what medical transition actually involves and why some trans people pursue it. What hormone therapy can and cannot change. What surgery costs, in recovery, risk and money. What gender dysphoria is, and why it is so hard to understand from the outside when you don't feel it yourself. Why the idea that it's just a whim or a trend struggles to explain why anyone would accept all of that. And why some trans people choose not to transition medically at all. This is the third video in a series about transgender people. The first asked why there suddenly seem to be so many trans people, the second how you know you're trans. The next one asks: why is it so hard to be trans?

entry.title: What If Everyone on Earth Owned a Car?
entry.summary: Imagine a world where every person on Earth owns a car. Not every family, every person. Eight billion people, eight billion cars. It sounds like the ultimate freedom, and it isn't as absurd as it sounds: in the United States there are already roughly eight vehicles for every ten people. So what would happen if every country reached the American level? This video works it out step by step: where eight billion cars would park, how many people one lane of a city street can actually move, what happened after Houston widened the Katy Freeway to more than twenty lanes, how many cars the world's factories would have to build every year, and how much petrol, or electricity, it would take to keep them all moving.

entry.title: How Do You Know You're Trans?
entry.summary: How do you know you're a man? Or a woman? Most people would simply say: I just know. They have never had to examine their gender identity, and nobody asks them to prove it. But what if that sense of certainty isn't there? This video looks at how people come to understand that they're trans. Why it is often a slow process rather than a single dramatic moment. Why some people start asking these questions in childhood or puberty, and others at thirty, forty or sixty. Why it is hard to recognise something you don't have a word for. And why not fitting gender stereotypes, or being attracted to people of the same sex, is not the same thing as being trans. It also looks at doubt, at people who suppress those feelings, at people who realise they're trans but decide not to transition, and at detransition: what it does and doesn't tell us.

entry.title: Why Can You Still Buy a Phone With a Keyboard?
entry.summary: 5G. A recent version of Android. Twelve gigabytes of memory. And a physical QWERTY keyboard. Not a ten-year-old BlackBerry from eBay, but a phone you can buy today. Touchscreens won this fight more than fifteen years ago. So why does a phone like this still exist? And who would actually want one? From BlackBerry to the Unihertz Titan, the Astro Slide, the F(x)tec Pro1 X and the Clicks Communicator: what can physical keys do that glass can't, why don't Samsung, Apple or Google make phones like this — and is the keyboard on a phone really dead?
